\subsubsection{Excitation and Averaging}\label{sss:eis-excitation}

The excitation is delivered as commanded only when its two codes lie inside one
octave. A \num{32}-code toggle asks for \SI{19.531}{\milli\volt} peak to peak;
measured at the DAC output it arrives \SI{0.03}{\percent} to
\SI{0.06}{\percent} high when neither code crosses a power-of-two boundary and
\SI{0.15}{\percent} to \SI{1.51}{\percent} low when the pair straddles one
(Table~\ref{tab:eis-excitation}). \textbf{The whole amplitude error is the
carry}: a pair that flips one or two bits delivers what it was told to within
\SI{0.06}{\percent}, a pair that flips eight bits is out by \SI{1.5}{\percent},
and at the \SI{4}{\milli\volt} excitation a carry at the most significant bit
costs \SI{-3.5}{\percent}. It is frequency-flat --- the same pair delivers the
same amplitude at \SI{100}{\hertz}, \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} and
\SI{10}{\kilo\hertz} in every printed digit --- so it is a static property of
the code pair, removed either by choosing the pair or by calibrating it once.

\paragraph{Two levels beat a synthesised sine.} For the same code excursion the
two-level square delivers \(1.28\times\) the fundamental of a stepped sine,
against \(4/\pi = \num{1.273}\) predicted, and the measured impedance is
identical for both to five significant figures --- \SI{11003.45}{\ohm} against
\SI{11003.52}{\ohm} at 8, 16 and 32 steps --- because the demodulator is
ratiometric and the excitation's shape cancels. The sine is also the less
accurate excitation, \SI{-2.4}{\percent} of amplitude against the square's
\SI{-1.5}{\percent}, since each of its steps visits a different code carrying its
own linearity error. The square costs less firmware and delivers
\SI{2.2}{\decibel} more signal.

\paragraph{Averaging buys \(\sqrt{N}\), and then stops at a bias.} Process gain
is exactly \(\sqrt{N}\) over four decades of record length: at the bottom gain
code an \SI{11}{\kilo\ohm} load reads \(\sigma/|Z| = \SI{1.20}{\percent}\) from
a single \SI{1}{\milli\second} cycle and \SI{0.0093}{\percent} from
\num{16384} cycles, every factor of four in record length being
\SI{6.02}{\decibel} to the last digit. Underneath it sits a deterministic
quantisation bias that averaging does not reduce at all: \(+\SI{1.94}{\percent}\)
at that bottom code, where the output fundamental is \num{13.7} converter codes,
and \(-\SI{0.56}{\percent}\) at the code that ranges the same load, where it is
\num{275}. The current channel's quantisation is dithered by \num{3.4} codes of
front-end noise and averages away; the potential channel carries no front-end
noise, so its quantisation is periodic with the excitation and lands in the
phasor as a bias. It cancels exactly in a ratio against a known impedance --- a
third independent reason for the calibration impedance, after the feedback pole
of Section~\ref{sss:eis-accuracy} and the code-pair error above.
